# UNIT 6: Seerah Madinah & the Building of a Community
## Student Handout (Age 10)
---
*“A Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hands people are safe.”* — Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him)

---

## Page 1: Welcome, Young Historian!

Welcome to your study guide for Unit 6! In this unit, we are going to travel back in time to the year 622 CE. We will follow our beloved Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) as he leaves his hometown of Makkah and travels to the city of Madinah. 

In Madinah, the Prophet (pbuh) didn't just build a place to pray; he built a beautiful, peaceful community where people of different tribes and religions could live together safely. 

As we study this journey, we will explore:
1.  **The Hijrah:** The secret escape and lessons in trust and sacrifice.
2.  **The Constitution of Madinah:** The peace treaty that united different groups.
3.  **Badr and Uhud:** Lessons in patience, discipline, and peaceful rules during war.
4.  **The Farewell Sermon:** The Prophet's final speech about equality and kindness.
5.  **The Golden Chain of Knowledge:** How knowledge traveled from the Companions to **Imam Malik** in Madinah.

### Fiqh & Creed Literacy
As a young scholar, you will see special boxes in this handout:
*   **Creed Focus (Aqidah):** Explaining our beliefs according to the **Ash'ari** school.
*   **Law Focus (Fiqh):** Explaining our actions according to the **Maliki** school.

Whenever you see a word in bold with *italics* in parentheses, that is an Arabic term. Make sure you read the explanation so you can start speaking like a true scholar!

---

## Page 2: The Command to Leave Makkah (What is Hijrah?)

For thirteen years in Makkah, the Muslims were treated very badly by the leaders of the Quraysh tribe. The Muslims were boycotted, teased, and even hurt just because they believed in One Allah. Yet, they stayed patient. 

Finally, the Quraysh leaders met at a place called *Dar al-Nadwah* (the assembly house) and made a terrible plan: they decided to choose one young man from every family to attack the Prophet (pbuh) at the same time. That way, the Prophet’s family wouldn’t be able to fight back against all the tribes at once.

But Allah is the Best of Planners. He sent the Angel Jibril (Gabriel) to tell the Prophet (pbuh) that it was time to migrate.

### What is Hijrah?
**Hijrah** (*Hijrah* - هِجْرَة) means migration or moving from one place to another for the sake of Allah to protect your faith. 

The Prophet (pbuh) chose a city named **Yathrib** as the new home. Yathrib was located about 280 miles north of Makkah. Later, this city would be named **Al-Madinah al-Munawwarah** (*Al-Madīnah al-Munawwarah* - الْمَدِينَة الْمُنَوَّرَة), which means "The Illuminated City."

To make this journey, the Muslims had to make huge sacrifices. They had to leave behind their houses, their wealth, and sometimes even their family members who did not believe. They did all of this because their faith was the most valuable thing they owned.

---

## Page 3: Doing Your Best & Trusting Allah (The Story of the Cave)

Before leaving Makkah, the Prophet (pbuh) made a very careful plan. He did not just walk out into the desert. He hired a skilled guide named Abdullah ibn Urayqit to show him secret paths. He and his best friend, Abu Bakr, decided to travel south instead of north to trick the Quraysh search parties. They also hid in a dark cave on Mount Thawr for three days.

This careful planning teaches us a very important lesson about how a Muslim should live.

> ### Creed Focus: Asbab (Causes) & Tawakkul (Trust)
> In the **Ash'ari** creed, we learn two major concepts:
> 1.  **Asbab** (*Asbāb* - أَسْبَاب): The physical means or steps we take (like wearing a seatbelt, studying for a test, or locking a door).
> 2.  **Tawakkul** (*Tawakkul* - تَوَكُّل): Placing our absolute trust and reliance on Allah alone for the final result.
> 
> **The Golden Rule:** We must use our bodies to take the necessary steps (*Asbab*), but our hearts must only rely on Allah. We must never believe that the physical steps *create* the result. Only Allah creates the result. 
> 
> If we ignore the steps and say, *"I trust Allah, so I won't study,"* we are being foolish. But if we study and say, *"My studying is what got me the A,"* we are forgetting that Allah is the Creator of our intelligence and our success.

While hiding in the cave, the Quraysh trackers walked right up to the entrance. Abu Bakr was terrified for the Prophet's safety. He whispered: *"If one of them looks down at his feet, he will see us."*
The Prophet (pbuh) calmly replied: *"O Abu Bakr, what do you think of two, of whom Allah is the third?"* (Quran 9:40). 

Allah sent a spider to spin a web across the cave entrance and a wild dove to lay eggs in a nest there. When the Quraysh saw this, they thought, *"No one could have entered this cave recently,"* and they left. Allah used a tiny spider web to protect His messenger!

---

## Page 4: Welcome to Madinah!

When the Prophet (pbuh) finally arrived in Quba', on the outskirts of Yathrib, the people were waiting for him with great joy. They sang songs of welcome. 

### 1. The Prophet's Camel and the Orphans' Land
As the Prophet (pbuh) entered the city, every tribe wanted him to live with them. They held the reins of his camel, **Al-Qaswa'** (*Al-Qaswā'* - الْقَصْوَاء). The Prophet (pbuh) said: *"Let her go, for she is commanded."* 
The camel walked and finally knelt down on a flat, empty piece of land. 

*   This land belonged to two young orphan brothers named Sahl and Suhayl.
*   The Prophet (pbuh) insisted on buying the land from them at a fair price, refusing to take it as a gift. 
*   **Fiqh Lesson:** In Islamic law, we must protect the property of orphans (*Aytām*) and never take advantage of them.

### 2. Building Al-Masjid al-Nabawi
On this land, they built the Prophet's Mosque (*Al-Masjid al-Nabawi* - الْمَسْجِد النَّبَوِيّ). It was simple, built from mud-bricks and palm trees. The Prophet (pbuh) worked right alongside the companions, carrying heavy bricks. The mosque was not just for prayer; it was a school, a community hall, and a place where the poor could sleep.

### 3. The Great Brotherhood (Al-Muwakhah)
The Muslims in Madinah were now divided into two groups:
*   **Al-Muhajirun** (*Al-Muhājirūn* - الْمُهَاجِرُونَ): The Emigrants who left Makkah with nothing.
*   **Al-Ansar** (*Al-Anṣār* - الأَنْصَار): The Helpers of Madinah who welcomed them.

The Prophet (pbuh) paired one Muhajir with one Ansari as brothers. The Ansar were so generous that they offered to share half of their homes, fields, and food with their new brothers. The Muhajirun accepted this love but immediately worked hard to support themselves, showing that a Muslim should always be independent and industrious.

---

## Page 5: The Constitution of Madinah

Now that different groups were living in the same city, the Prophet (pbuh) did something amazing. He wrote a document called the **Constitution of Madinah** (*Wathīqat al-Madīnah* - وَثِيقَة الْمَدِينَة). This was the first written constitution in the history of the world!

It was a treaty signed by the Muslims and the Jewish tribes of Madinah. It set down rules so everyone could live together in peace.

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                THE CONSTITUTION OF MADINAH                  |
|                        Key Pillars:                         |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|  1. ONE COMMUNITY: Muslims and Jews are part of one city,   |
|     promising to defend it together if attacked.            |
|                                                             |
|  2. FREEDOM OF FAITH: "The Jews have their religion and     |
|     the Muslims have theirs." No one is forced to convert.  |
|                                                             |
|  3. JUSTICE FOR ALL: Helping the oppressed and stopping     |
|     criminals, even if the criminal is a close relative.    |
|                                                             |
|  4. PEACE COVENANT: No citizen is allowed to help the       |
|     enemies of the city (like the hostile Quraysh).         |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
```

This constitution teaches us that Muslims are builders of peace. We must respect the rights of our neighbors, even if they pray differently than we do.

---

## Page 6: Fiqh of Treaties and Safety (Maliki Rules)

The Constitution of Madinah was not just a political agreement; it became a part of Islamic law. In the **Maliki** school of jurisprudence, keeping agreements and protecting others are sacred duties.

Let's look at two important terms that Imam Malik explained in his books:

### 1. Aman (Safety / Protection)
**Aman** (*Amān* - أَمَان) means granting safety to someone. In the Maliki school, if *any* Muslim—even a normal citizen, a woman, or a young person—gives their word to a non-Muslim traveler that they are safe, the entire Muslim community and the government must respect that safety. 
Imam Malik wrote that even if a Muslim just makes a friendly gesture that looks like safety to a non-Muslim, that person is legally protected under *Aman*. This shows how much Islam values human life and the word of a believer.

### 2. 'Ahd (Covenant / Treaty)
**'Ahd** (*'Ahd* - عَهْد) is a sacred promise or treaty. 
*   **Rule:** It is strictly forbidden (*Harām*) to break a treaty.
*   **Treachery (Ghadr):** If we sign a peace treaty with another community, we cannot attack them or trick them while the treaty is active. The Prophet (pbuh) said: *"For every betrayer, a banner will be raised on the Day of Resurrection to show their treachery."*

---

## Page 7: Badr & Uhud: Lessons in Patience

For many years, the pagan Quraysh continued to threaten the Muslims, stealing the property they left behind in Makkah and blocking them from trading. To stop this aggression, Allah finally gave the Muslims permission to defend themselves.

### 1. The Battle of Badr (2 AH)
The Quraysh marched toward Madinah with 1,000 well-armed soldiers. The Muslims had only 313 men and very few weapons. 
Before the battle, the Prophet (pbuh) did not boast. Instead, he spent the night weeping and praying to Allah, asking for help. The next day, the Muslims won a miraculous victory. 

> ### Creed Focus: Where Does Victory Come From?
> In the **Ash'ari** creed, we believe that Allah is **Al-Nasir** (*Al-Nāṣir* - النَّاصِر) — The Giver of Victory. 
> At Badr, the Quran says: *"And you threw not when you threw, but it was Allah who threw..."* (Quran 8:17). 
> The Prophet (pbuh) threw a handful of sand toward the enemy (the physical cause), but Allah made that sand enter the eyes of the enemy army (the ultimate effect). The lesson is: victory does not come from having more weapons or money; it comes only from Allah when we obey Him.

### 2. The Battle of Uhud (3 AH)
One year later, the Quraysh returned with 3,000 soldiers. The Prophet (pbuh) placed 50 archers on a hill and gave them a strict command: *"Do not leave this hill, even if you see birds eating our bodies, until I send for you."*
During the battle, the Muslims were winning. The archers saw the physical spoils of war (*Ghanīmah* - غَنِيمَة) on the ground. Forgetting the Prophet's command, most of them ran down to collect the items. 
Because they left their post, the enemy cavalry swept around the hill and attacked the Muslims from behind, causing a major setback where many companions were killed. 

**The Lesson:** Disobeying the Prophet's commands because we want worldly things (*Dunyā*) always leads to failure.

---

## Page 8: Rules of Peace and Battle

In many ancient cultures, war meant destroying everything: burning houses, killing families, and ruining fields. But the Prophet (pbuh) taught that conflict must never be glorified. It is only a last resort to stop oppression.

Imam Malik recorded the strict rules of combat that the first Caliph, Abu Bakr, gave to his army based on the Prophet's teachings:

```
                  +--------------------------------+
                  |    MALIKI ETHICS OF WARFARE    |
                  +--------------------------------+
                                  |
         +------------------------+------------------------+
         |                                                 |
         v                                                 v
+------------------+                              +------------------+
| PROTECT PEOPLE   |                              | PROTECT NATURE   |
| * No killing of  |                              | * No cutting of  |
|   women/children |                              |   fruitful trees |
| * No hurting the |                              | * No burning of  |
|   elderly/sick   |                              |   crops/fields   |
| * No attacking   |                              | * No slaughter of|
|   monks/priests  |                              |   animals except |
|   in temples     |                              |   for food       |
+------------------+                              +------------------+
```

These rules were written 1,300 years before modern international treaties like the Geneva Conventions! They show that even when Muslims are forced to defend themselves, they must be kind, fair, and protect the environment.

---

## Page 9: The Farewell Sermon (Khutbat al-Wada')

In the tenth year after the Hijrah, the Prophet (pbuh) performed his final pilgrimage to Makkah. He stood on Mount Arafat and gave a beautiful, final speech to over 100,000 Muslims. This speech is called **Khutbat al-Wada'** (*Khutbat al-Wadā'* - خُطْبَة الْوَدَاع).

In this sermon, the Prophet (pbuh) summarized the core values of Islam:

1.  **Sanctity of Life and Property:** The life and wealth of every human being is sacred. It is a major sin to steal or hurt someone.
2.  **No Racism:** The Prophet (pbuh) declared: *"An Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab, nor does a non-Arab have any superiority over an Arab. A white person has no superiority over a black person, nor does a black person have any superiority over a white person, except by piety (Taqwa)."*
3.  **Kindness to Women:** He commanded men to treat women with gentleness and respect, calling them a trust (*Amānah*) from Allah.
4.  **Economic Justice:** He abolished **Riba** (*Ribā* - رِبًا), which is usury or lending money at high interest. This system kept poor people in debt while making rich people richer.

---

## Page 10: How Knowledge Traveled to Madinah

Have you ever wondered how we know all these details today? It is because of a beautiful chain of teachers and students that started in Madinah.

1.  **The Source:** The Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) lived, taught, and passed away in Madinah.
2.  **The Companions:** Great Sahabah like **Abdullah ibn Umar** (the son of Umar) and **Aisha** (the Prophet's wife) lived in Madinah and taught thousands of students.
3.  **The Tabi'un:** The next generation of scholars, including the **Seven Fiqh Scholars of Madinah**, collected these teachings. A famous teacher among them was **Nafi'**, who was the personal student of Ibn Umar.
4.  **Imam Malik:** Imam Malik ibn Anas was born in Madinah. He studied under Nafi' and Rabi'at al-Ra'y. Because he lived in the very city where the Prophet walked, he wrote down the city's continuous practices (*'Amal*) in his book, **Al-Muwatta** (*Al-Muwaṭṭa'* - الْمُوَطَّأ). 

This is why the Maliki school is so unique: it is built on the living inheritance of the people of Madinah.

---

### Reflection Question: Let's Think!
The Prophet (pbuh) had the power to make Yathrib a city *only* for Muslims, but instead he chose to write a constitution that protected the religious rights of Jewish tribes and other communities. 
*   *If you were to create a "classroom constitution" for your school or family today, what rules would you write to make sure everyone—regardless of their background or differences—feels safe, respected, and included? How does this connect to what you learned about the Prophet's character?*

---

### Sources & Bibliography

2.  *Al-Shifa bi Ta'rif Huquq al-Mustafa* (The Cure through the Rights of the Chosen One) by Qadi 'Ayyad.
3.  *Al-Seerah al-Nabawiyyah* (The Life of the Prophet) by Ibn Hisham.
4.  *Fiqh al-Seerah* (Jurisprudence of the Biography) by Sheikh Muhammad al-Ghazali.

# Assessment Questions: Seerah Madinah & the Building of a Community
## For Student Handout (Age 10)
---

### Part A: Multiple Choice (10 Questions)
*Select the best answer for each question.*

1.  **What does the word Hijrah (هِجْرَة) mean in Islamic history?**
    *   a) A vacation to another country.
    *   b) Migration for the sake of Allah to protect one's faith.
    *   c) Running away from a battle.
    *   d) Going on a business trip.

2.  **Which city was renamed Al-Madinah al-Munawwarah (The Illuminated City)?**
    *   a) Makkah
    *   b) Yathrib
    *   c) Quba'
    *   d) Ta'if

3.  **According to the Ash'ari creed, what are Asbab (أَسْبَاب)?**
    *   a) The miracles performed by prophets.
    *   b) The physical, worldly means or steps we are commanded to take.
    *   c) The bad deeds that dry out the heart.
    *   d) The rules of inheritance in Islamic law.

4.  **If you study hard for a test, what does the Ash'ari creed teach about your grade?**
    *   a) Your studying itself created the A grade.
    *   b) Only Allah creates the result, but you must study because He commanded you to use the physical means.
    *   c) You do not need to study because Allah has already decided your grade anyway.
    *   d) Studying is forbidden because it shows you don't trust Allah.

5.  **Which animal chose the site of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah?**
    *   a) A horse
    *   b) A sheep
    *   c) The Prophet's camel, Al-Qaswa'
    *   d) A dove

6.  **Who were Al-Ansar (الأَنْصَار) in Madinah?**
    *   a) The traders who came from Makkah.
    *   b) The Helpers of Madinah who welcomed the Emigrants.
    *   c) The non-Muslim tribes who refused to sign treaties.
    *   d) The scholars who wrote down the Quran.

7.  **What is the Constitution of Madinah (Wathiqat al-Madinah)?**
    *   a) A map of the city.
    *   b) A treaty signed by Muslims and Jewish tribes to live together in peace.
    *   c) A list of the seven obligations of Wudu.
    *   d) The names of the early Companions.

8.  **According to the Maliki school, what is Aman (أَمَان)?**
    *   a) A fast performed on Mondays.
    *   b) The legal act of granting safety or protection to a non-Muslim.
    *   c) The collection of charity for orphans.
    *   d) A type of prayer posture.

9.  **According to Ash'ari creed, who is Al-Nasir (النَّاصِر)?**
    *   a) The ruler of Madinah.
    *   b) The Giver of Victory (Allah).
    *   c) The helper who carries the water.
    *   d) The leader of the archers.

10. **Which of these is strictly FORBIDDEN in warfare according to Maliki ethics?**
    *   a) Defending yourself against an army.
    *   b) Cutting down fruitful trees and destroying crops.
    *   c) Praying during battle.
    *   d) Offering peace treaties to the enemy.

---

### Part B: Scenario-Based Questions (5 Questions)
*Read the scenario and choose or write the correct response based on what you have learned.*

11. **Imran wants to get a good grade on his Quran test. He says, "I have Tawakkul (trust) in Allah, so I don't need to study. Allah will give me an A." How should you correct Imran using the Ash'ari creed?**
    *   *Answer:* You should tell Imran that true trust (*Tawakkul*) requires using the physical means (*Asbab*) that Allah created. Ignoring the means (not studying) is foolishness (*Sufah*). He must study hard with his body, but trust in Allah with his heart for the result.

12. **Zainab is writing a contract for a school project. She remembers the Constitution of Madinah and wants to include her non-Muslim class partners fairly. What lesson from the Constitution can she apply?**
    *   *Answer:* Zainab can apply the lesson of **coexistence and freedom of faith**. The Constitution of Madinah showed that people of different beliefs can form a single community (*Ummah*) for mutual help and joint goals, treating each other with equal justice.

13. **During a friendly soccer match, Amina's team is winning. The referee makes a mistake, and the other team gets a penalty kick. Amina gets angry and says, "Let's cheat on the next play to make it fair." How does this violate the Prophetic lessons of Uhud?**
    *   *Answer:* In Uhud, when the archers disobeyed the Prophet's instructions because they wanted the spoils of war (*Ghanimah*), it led to a major defeat. Disobeying rules for worldly gain or cheating always ruins the community. A Muslim must be patient (*Sabr*) and follow rules honestly.

14. **Yousef finds out that some people are cutting down olive trees in a park during a protest. He remembers the military rules codified by Imam Malik. Why would Yousef argue that this action is against Islamic ethics?**
    *   *Answer:* In Maliki fiqh, the ethics of engagement are so strict that even during a defensive war, the Prophet (pbuh) and Caliph Abu Bakr banned the cutting down of fruitful trees or the destruction of crops. If destroying nature is banned during war, it is certainly banned during times of peace.

15. **A non-Muslim student travels to a Muslim country as a tourist. According to the Maliki ruling on Aman (safety), what is the duty of the citizens toward this tourist?**
    *   *Answer:* The citizens have a duty to protect and respect the tourist. In Maliki fiqh, if a visitor is granted *Aman* (safety) by a covenant, it is a sacred obligation (*'Ahd*) that cannot be broken. Doing them harm would be treachery (*Ghadr*), which is a major sin.

---

### Part C: Short Answer & Matching (5 Questions)
*Answer the questions briefly or match the terms.*

16. **Match the Arabic term to its correct English meaning:**
    *   1. *Ansar* -> ______ (Answer: The Helpers of Madinah)
    *   2. *Muhajirun* -> ______ (Answer: The Emigrants from Makkah)
    *   3. *Niyyah* -> ______ (Answer: The inner intention of the heart)
    *   4. *Riba* -> ______ (Answer: Usury or high interest, which is forbidden)

17. **What did the Prophet (pbuh) say about racism in his Farewell Sermon?**
    *   *Answer:* He declared that no race is superior to another (Arab or non-Arab, white or black), and that the only thing that makes one person better than another in the sight of Allah is their piety (*Taqwa*).

18. **Why did the Prophet (pbuh) insist on buying the land for Al-Masjid al-Nabawi from the two orphans instead of taking it as a gift?**
    *   *Answer:* To establish the legal rule that the rights and property of orphans (*Aytam*) must be protected with absolute justice and never taken advantage of.

19. **What is the Golden Chain (Silsilat al-Dhahab) of knowledge that links the Prophet (pbuh) to Imam Malik?**
    *   *Answer:* It is the direct chain of transmission: Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) -> Abdullah ibn Umar -> Nafi' (the student of Ibn Umar) -> Imam Malik.

20. **Why did Imam Malik believe that the Practice of the People of Madinah ('Amal Ahl al-Madinah) is a strong source of law?**
    *   *Answer:* Because the children of the Companions in Madinah learned their daily actions directly from their parents, who learned from the Prophet (pbuh). This continuous living practice represents the Sunnah in action.

### Part B: Scenario-Based Questions (5 Questions)

If destroying nature is banned during war, it is certainly banned during times of peace.

    *   *Answer:* Because the children of the Companions in Madinah learned their daily actions directly from their parents, who learned from the Prophet (pbuh). This continuous living practice represents the Sunnah in action.

# UNIT 6: Seerah Madinah & the Building of a Community
## Student Handout (Age 13)
---
*“Whoever harms a covenant-partner (Mu'ahid) has harmed me, and whoever harms me has angered Allah.”* — Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him)

---

## Page 1: Introduction: Establishing the Divine Community

Welcome, young scholar, to this comprehensive study guide for Unit 6. In this unit, we shift our focus from the Makkan period of the Prophetic biography (*Seerah*) to the Madinan period. 

In Makkah, the early Muslims were a persecuted minority. The focus of revelation and practice was primarily on **Tawheed** (the absolute oneness of Allah) and internalizing personal belief (*Aqidah*). The Muslims did not possess a political structure or legal code. 

With the migration (**Hijrah**) to Madinah, the message of Islam matured from personal faith into the establishment of a sacred, model community. In Madinah, the Prophet (pbuh) established:
*   A legal system (*Fiqh*) governing business, family, and international relations.
*   A political covenant (the Constitution of Madinah) managing relations between diverse faith groups.
*   Rules of defensive warfare and ethics of engagement.
*   A system of knowledge transmission that would eventually form the basis of the **Maliki** school of law.

This handout will analyze these developments through the lens of **Ash'ari** theology and **Maliki** jurisprudence. 

### Developing Fiqh Literacy
As you read, pay close attention to:
*   **Ash'ari Creed Focus:** How our theological understanding of destiny (*Qadar*), cause and effect (*Asbab*), and Divine attributes explains the events of Seerah.
*   **Maliki Jurisprudence Focus:** How specific laws, treaties, and rules of engagement were derived by Imam Malik and the early scholars of Madinah.
*   **Arabic Terminology:** Learn the precise vocabulary used by Muslim historians and jurists.

---

## Page 2: The Hijrah: The Theology of Asbab and Tawakkul

The migration from Makkah to Madinah (known as the **Hijrah** - هِجْرَة) in 622 CE is a watershed moment in Islamic history. So significant was this event that the second Caliph, Umar ibn al-Khattab, established it as the beginning of the Islamic calendar (AH - *Anno Hegirae*).

However, the Hijrah is not merely a historical migration; it is a profound lesson in the relationship between human effort and Divine Will.

> ### Creed Focus: Cause & Effect (Asbab) and Reliance (Tawakkul)
> A core debate in Islamic theology concerns how physical actions relate to outcomes. The **Ash'ari** school teaches a balanced path:
> 
> 1.  **Asbab** (*Asbāb* - أَسْبَاب, singular: *Sabab*): These are the physical causes or worldly means (e.g., eating food to satisfy hunger, preparing weapons for defense, locking a door for safety).
> 2.  **Tawakkul** (*Tawakkul* - تَوَكُّل): This is the absolute trust and reliance of the heart on Allah alone as the Creator of all things.
> 
> **The Ash'ari Rule:** Allah is the sole Creator of both causes and effects. The physical cause does *not* possess the independent, natural power to create the effect. Fire does not burn by its own power; rather, Allah creates the burning *at the moment* the fire touches the wood. 
> 
> Therefore, a Muslim is legally commanded to use the physical means (*Asbab*) out of obedience to Allah's natural laws, but must never rely on those means. 
> *   To rely *only* on the means is a form of hidden association (*Shirk Khafi*), as it attributes creative power to objects.
> *   To ignore the means while claiming "trust in Allah" is foolishness (*Sufah*) and disobedience, as it mocks the order Allah established in the universe.

### The Prophet's Practical Application of Asbab
When the Prophet (pbuh) migrated, he demonstrated perfect Ash'ari theology:
*   He did not simply walk out into the open desert expecting a miracle. He utilized every physical *Sabab* available.
*   He hired an expert guide, Abdullah ibn Urayqit (who was a non-Muslim, proving that worldly expertise should be sought regardless of faith).
*   He hid in the Cave of Thawr for three days until the search parties grew tired.
*   He had Abu Bakr's shepherd, Amir ibn Fuhayrah, drive sheep behind them to erase their tracks.

Yet, when the Quraysh stood at the mouth of the cave, and Abu Bakr feared they would be caught, the Prophet (pbuh) did not look to his physical preparations. He pointed directly to the Ultimate Cause (*Al-Musabbib*): *"O Abu Bakr, what do you think of two, of whom Allah is the third?"* (Quran 9:40).

---

## Page 3: Sacrifice, Intention (Niyyah), and Brotherhood

To migrate, the Companions had to sacrifice everything. Many left behind spouses, children, houses, and businesses. 

### The Law of Intention (Niyyah)
In Islamic law, the value of an action is determined by its inner motive. This is called **Niyyah** (*Niyyah* - نِيَّة).
The Prophet (pbuh) said in a famous Hadith:
> *"Actions are only by intentions, and every person will have only what they intended. So, whoever's migration (Hijrah) was for Allah and His Messenger, their migration was for Allah and His Messenger. And whoever's migration was for some worldly gain or to marry a woman, their migration was for that which they migrated."* (Sahih al-Bukhari & Muslim).

This Hadith teaches that two people can perform the exact same physical action (traveling 280 miles through the desert), yet one receives the highest reward from Allah, while the other receives nothing, because of their internal *Niyyah*.

### Reconstructing Society: The Muwakhah
Upon arriving in Yathrib—which the Prophet (pbuh) renamed **Al-Madinah al-Munawwarah** (The Illuminated City)—he faced a massive refugee crisis. The Emigrants (**Al-Muhajirun** - الْمُهَاجِرُونَ) had arrived with no capital, while the local helpers (**Al-Ansar** - الأَنْصَار) owned the agricultural lands.

To solve this, the Prophet (pbuh) established the **Muwakhah** (*Muwākhāh* - الْمُؤَاخَاة) — a formal, legally binding covenant of brotherhood pairing one Muhajir with one Ansari. 
*   The Ansar offered to divide their wealth, lands, and homes in half.
*   The Muhajirun accepted this brotherhood but maintained their economic dignity. Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, when offered half of his Ansari brother's wealth, replied: *"May Allah bless your wealth and your family. Just show me the way to the market."* Within a short time, he became one of the wealthiest merchants in Madinah.

---

## Page 4: Wathiqat al-Madinah (The Constitution)

Madinah was not a homogeneous town; it was a complex tribal society composed of two major pagan Arab tribes (Aws and Khazraj), three major Jewish tribes (Banu Qaynuqa', Banu al-Nadir, and Banu Qurayzah), and the newly arrived Makkan Muslims.

To govern this diverse society, the Prophet (pbuh) drafted **Wathiqat al-Madinah** (*Wathīqat al-Madīnah* - وَثِيقَة الْمَدِينَة) — the Constitution of Madinah. Written in 622 CE, it is recognized by historians as the first written constitution in human history.

```
       +-----------------------------------------------------------+
       |             THE CIVIC MATRIX OF THE CONSTITUTION          |
       +-----------------------------------------------------------+
                                     |
         +---------------------------+---------------------------+
         |                                                       |
         v                                                       v
+------------------+                                    +------------------+
|   CIVIC RIGHTS   |                                    |   CIVIC DUTIES   |
| * Freedom of     |                                    | * Shared defense |
|   Religion       |                                    |   of the city    |
| * Absolute equal |                                    | * No alliances   |
|   justice        |                                    |   with enemies   |
| * Protection of  |                                    | * Collective tax |
|   property       |                                    |   for war costs  |
+------------------+                                    +------------------+
```

### The Concept of Ummah in the Constitution
Crucially, the Constitution declared that the Muslims and the Jewish tribes who signed the agreement formed **Ummah Wahidah** (*Ummah Wāḥidah* - أُمَّة وَاحِدَة) — a single, unified civic community. 
*   *"The Jews of Banu Awf are a community (Ummah) alongside the believers. The Jews have their religion, and the Muslims have theirs."*
*   This document demonstrates that a state can be Islamic in its authority, yet pluralistic and protective of non-Muslim citizens' rights.

---

## Page 5: Fiqh of Safety (Aman) and Treaties ('Ahd)

In the **Maliki** school of jurisprudence, the laws of international relations and treaties are based directly on the historical actions of the Prophet (pbuh) in Madinah. Imam Malik codified these rules under two major categories:

### 1. The Legality of Aman (Safety)
**Aman** (*Amān* - أَمَان) is the granting of asylum or safe passage to a non-Muslim. 
*   **Maliki Ruling:** In the Maliki school, *any* free Muslim citizen—whether male or female, rich or poor—has the legal authority to grant *Aman* to a non-Muslim traveler or diplomat. Once a citizen grants safety, the entire state and the army are legally bound to protect that person.
*   Imam Malik ruled that even if a Muslim merely points or makes a physical gesture of peace that a non-Muslim interprets as safety, the *Aman* is valid and legally binding. 

### 2. The Sanctity of 'Ahd (Covenant)
**'Ahd** (*'Ahd* - عَهْد) refers to a treaty or peace agreement. 
*   **Maliki Ruling:** Breaking a treaty is classified as a major sin and a legal crime. If a treaty is active between the Islamic state and another community, Muslims are strictly forbidden from committing **Ghadr** (*Ghadr* - غَدْر) — treachery or surprise attacks.
*   If the state fears that the other side is about to betray the treaty, they cannot attack them secretly. The Quran commands that the treaty must be formally dissolved first, so both sides are on equal terms: *"And if you fear treachery from a people, throw back [their covenant] to them on equal terms. Indeed, Allah does not love the treacherous"* (Quran 8:58).

---

## Page 6: Badr & Uhud: Decree, Failure, and Patience

For thirteen years in Makkah, Muslims were forbidden from physical combat (*Qital*). They were commanded to control their hands and establish prayer. In Madinah, after being driven from their homes and losing their properties, Allah revealed the permission to fight back defensively:
> *"Permission [to fight] has been given to those who are being fought, because they were wronged. And indeed, Allah is competent to give them victory."* (Quran 22:39).

This sets the stage for the battles of Badr and Uhud, which were tests of spiritual discipline rather than struggles for power.

### Badr (2 AH): The Test of Certainty (Yaqeen)
At Badr, the Muslims were severely outnumbered (313 against 1,000). 
*   **Aqidah Connection:** The victory at Badr was a demonstration of Divine Will. Allah sent angels, not because He needed them, but to bring **Sakinah** (tranquility) to the hearts of the believers. 
*   The Quranic verse: *"And you threw not when you threw, but it was Allah who threw..."* (Quran 8:17) explains that while human acquisition (*Kasb*) performs the action, the ultimate creation of the effect belongs to Allah.

### Uhud (3 AH): The Test of Obedience
At Uhud, the Prophet (pbuh) placed 50 archers on Mount Aynayn to guard the army's rear. He gave them an absolute command not to leave under any circumstances. 
*   When the battle initially went in favor of the Muslims, the archers saw the physical spoils of war (**Ghanimah** - غَنِيمَة). Tempted by worldly wealth (*Dunya*), they disobeyed the command and ran down the hill.
*   The Quraysh cavalry seized this opening, circled the mountain, and attacked from behind, resulting in heavy losses for the Muslims and the wounding of the Prophet (pbuh) himself.

**The Theological Lesson:** Uhud proved that physical preparation without spiritual obedience leads to disaster. It also demonstrated the human nature of the Prophet (pbuh)—he could be wounded and bleed—showing that he is a messenger of Allah, not a divine entity.

---

## Page 7: Just War Theory & the Maliki Military Code

Islamic jurisprudence does not glorify war. War is viewed as a painful necessity to remove tyranny and protect religious freedom. The **Maliki** school contains some of the strictest rules in Islamic history regarding the ethics of conflict, derived directly from the Prophetic Sunnah and the commands of the first Caliph, Abu Bakr.

### The Maliki Code of Combat:
In his book *Al-Muwatta*, Imam Malik recorded the instructions given to the Muslim armies. These rules form the basis of Islamic Just War Theory:

1.  **Sanctity of Non-Combatants:** It is strictly prohibited to target or kill women, children, the elderly, the sick, and disabled persons.
2.  **Protection of Religious Freedom:** Monks, priests, and anyone dedicating themselves to worship in their temples, churches, or synagogues must be left completely alone. Their places of worship cannot be damaged.
3.  **Sanctity of Nature:** Cut down no fruitful trees, burn no fields of grain, and do not destroy crops.
4.  **No Scorched-Earth Policies:** Do not ruin wells, poison water supplies, or destroy buildings, houses, or towns.
5.  **Sanctity of Animals:** Do not slaughter sheep, cows, or camels except for what is necessary for food. Killing animals to ruin the enemy's economy is strictly forbidden.

### Comparison with Modern History
These rules were codified in Madinah in the 2nd century Hijri (8th century CE). By contrast, modern international laws, such as the Geneva Conventions, were only formulated in the mid-20th century. Islam established environmental protection and human rights in warfare over a thousand years prior.

---

## Page 8: The Farewell Sermon & the Five Necessities

In 10 AH (632 CE), the Prophet (pbuh) led his final pilgrimage, known as **Hajj al-Wada'** (*Ḥajj al-Wadā'* - حَجّ الْوَدَاع). At Mount Arafat, he delivered his historic Farewell Sermon (**Khutbat al-Wada'** - خُطْبَة الْوَدَاع) to over 100,000 companions.

This sermon served as a grand summary of the social, economic, and moral laws of Islam.

### The Five Necessities (Al-Daruriyyat al-Khams)
Islamic jurists, particularly in the Maliki school, note that this sermon established the protection of the **Five Necessities** (*Al-Ḍarūriyyāt al-Khams* - الضَّرُورِيَّات الْخَمْس), which are the core objectives of the Shariah (*Maqasid*):

1.  **Preservation of Life (*Hifz al-Nafs*):** The Prophet (pbuh) declared: *"Indeed, your blood and your property are sacred to you, like the sacredness of this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this city of yours."*
2.  **Preservation of Wealth (*Hifz al-Mal*):** He explicitly prohibited **Riba** (*Ribā* - رِبًا) — usury/interest. He declared all past usury canceled, starting with that of his uncle, Abbas. This stopped rich lenders from exploiting poor debtors, protecting economic wealth.
3.  **Preservation of Lineage and Family (*Hifz al-Nasl*):** He commanded men to treat women with absolute justice: *"Fear Allah concerning women, for you have taken them as a trust (Amanah) from Allah."*
4.  **Preservation of Honor (*Hifz al-'Ird*):** He forbade slander and tribalism, declaring that all human beings are descendants of Adam, and Adam was from dust.
5.  **Preservation of Religion (*Hifz al-Din*):** He urged the Muslims to hold fast to the Quran and Sunnah, warning them that while the devil could no longer make them worship idols, he would try to ruin their faith through small, division-causing sins.

---

## Page 9: How Knowledge Traveled: Amal Ahl al-Madinah

How did these legal rulings and historical facts reach us with such precision? 

In the **Maliki** school, the answer lies in a unique methodology called **'Amal Ahl al-Madinah** (*'Amal Ahl al-Madīnah* - عَمَل أَهْل الْمَدِينَة) — the Practice of the People of Madinah.

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|             THE GOLDEN CHAIN OF TRANSMISSION                |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                                             |
|   1. THE SOURCE: Prophet Muhammad (pbuh)                    |
|      (Lived, ruled, and taught in Madinah for 10 years)     |
|                               |                             |
|                               v                             |
|   2. THE COMPANIONS: Ibn Umar, Aisha, Zayd ibn Thabit       |
|      (Observed the Sunnah daily and taught the city)        |
|                               |                             |
|                               v                             |
|   3. THE TABI'UN: The Seven Fiqh Scholars / Nafi'           |
|      (Consolidated the laws and practices of the Sahabah)   |
|                               |                             |
|                               v                             |
|   4. THE COMPILER: Imam Malik ibn Anas                      |
|      (Codified these practices into the Maliki Madhhab)     |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### Why Imam Malik Valued 'Amal
Imam Malik argued that the continuous, daily practice of the people of Madinah was more reliable than a single written report (*Khabar al-Wahid*). 
His logic was:
*   If 10,000 people in a city are performing an action (such as letting their arms hang naturally in prayer—**Sadl**, or calling the Adhan in a specific way) because they saw their fathers do it, who saw the Sahabah do it, who saw the Prophet (pbuh) do it, this is a mass-transmitted, living Sunnah (*Mutawatir*).
*   A written report from one person might contain a mistake, but a whole city of scholars cannot collectively forget how the Prophet (pbuh) prayed and lived among them.

---

## Page 10: Synthesis & Critical Engagement

By studying the Seerah in Madinah, we learn that building a community requires:
1.  **Spiritual Alignment:** Acting upon physical means (*Asbab*) while maintaining absolute trust (*Tawakkul*) in Allah.
2.  **Civic Cooperation:** Developing covenants of peace and justice with people of other backgrounds.
3.  **Spiritual Discipline:** Understanding that patience (*Sabr*) and obedience are the roots of victory.
4.  **Scientific Inheritance:** Valuing the living chain of knowledge passed down through generations.

---

### Reflection Question: For Critical Analysis
The Constitution of Madinah established a civic alliance between Muslims and Jewish tribes based on mutual defense and religious freedom, even though they held different beliefs about creed (*Aqidah*) and theology. 
*   *Based on this historical model, analyze how a modern Muslim community living in a non-Muslim majority country should balance their religious identity (maintaining their creed and values) with their civic duties (cooperating with non-Muslim neighbors for the common good, such as charity, local laws, and environmental protection). What are the boundaries, and what are the opportunities for cooperation? Use the concepts of 'Ahd (covenant) and Aman (safety) to support your argument.*

---

2.  *Al-Shifa bi Ta'rif Huquq al-Mustafa* (The Cure through the Rights of the Chosen One) by Qadi 'Ayyad al-Yahsubi.
3.  *Al-Seerah al-Nabawiyyah* (The Life of the Prophet) by Ibn Hisham.
4.  *Al-Risalah* of Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani (classical Maliki manual).
5.  *Jawharat al-Tawheed* (The Jewel of Creed) by Imam Ibrahim al-Laqani.
6.  *Fiqh al-Seerah* (Jurisprudence of the Biography) by Sheikh Muhammad al-Ghazali.
7.  *Muhammad: His Life Based on the Earliest Sources* by Martin Lings.

# Presentation Slides: Seerah Madinah & the Building of a Community
## A Guide for Teachers (Maliki Fiqh & Ash'ari Aqidah)

---

# Slide 1: Welcome & Course Overview
## Building the Sacred Community
*   **Subject:** Islamic History (*Seerah*) and Jurisprudence (*Fiqh*)
*   **Fiqh School:** Maliki (*Madhhab*)
*   **Creed School:** Ash'ari (*Aqidah*)
*   **Core Focus:** Understanding the migration (*Hijrah*) to Madinah, the founding of the Islamic state, the rules of peaceful coexistence, the reality of defensive warfare, and the transmission of knowledge down to Imam Malik.
*   **Key Themes:**
    *   Trust in Allah (*Tawakkul*) and using physical means (*Asbab*)
    *   The Constitution of Madinah (*Wathiqat al-Madinah*)
    *   Patience in trials: Badr and Uhud
    *   The Farewell Sermon and the five necessities of Shariah (*Al-Daruriyyat al-Khams*)
    *   The Practice of the People of Madinah (*'Amal Ahl al-Madinah*)

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Welcome & Objective:** Welcome the students to this unit. Explain that this course moves from the Makkan period (which focused on personal belief in Tawheed) to the Madinan period, where those beliefs were put into action to build a community.
*   **Pedagogical Note:** Highlight that we study the Seerah not just as historical events, but as the foundation of our *Fiqh* (law) and *Aqidah* (creed). We will pay special attention to the rulings of the Maliki school and theological explanations of the Ash'ari school to show how classical scholars derived truth from the Prophet's life.
*   **Discussion Starter:** Ask the class: *"If you were starting a brand new town with people of different religions, what is the very first rule or agreement you would make?"*

---

# Slide 2: Fiqh & Aqidah Framework: The Madinan Context
## Connecting History to Belief and Practice
*   **Aqidah (Creed) Context:**
    *   The transition from forming the creed (*Tawheed*) in Makkah to manifesting it in community life.
    *   Understanding Divine Decree (*Qadar*) in times of victory and defeat.
*   **Fiqh (Law) Context:**
    *   Madinah is the birthplace of the Sunnah's practical implementation.
    *   Imam Malik’s jurisprudence is built on the living practice of this very city (*'Amal Ahl al-Madinah*).
*   **Seerah as Law:**
    *   The actions, treaties, and battles of the Prophet (pbuh) in Madinah became the legal bases for international relations, contracts, and governance.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Explanation:** Explain that in Makkah, Muslims had no state or political power; they focused on purifying their hearts and establishing *Aqidah*. In Madinah, Allah established them in the land. Thus, laws (*Fiqh*) regarding family, business, treaties, and community cooperation were revealed.
*   **Ash'ari/Maliki Link:** Emphasize that for Malikis, the customs and continuous practice of Madinah's early generations are highly authoritative. This is because they inherited their daily practices directly from the Prophet (pbuh) without interruption.

---

# Slide 3: The Call to Hijrah
## The Decision to Migrate
*   **Persecution in Makkah:**
    *   The Quraysh boycott, torture, and final plot to assassinate the Prophet (pbuh).
*   **The Command to Migrate (*Hijrah*):**
    *   *Hijrah* (هِجْرَة) means migration for the sake of Allah to preserve one's faith.
*   **The Destiny: Yathrib:**
    *   The Pledges of 'Aqabah (*Bay'at al-'Aqabah*) established a covenant of protection between the Prophet (pbuh) and the leaders of Yathrib.
*   **Sacrifice of the Companions (*Sahabah*):**
    *   Leaving homes, wealth, and families behind in Makkah solely for the pleasure of Allah.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Historical Context:** Explain how the pagan Quraysh decided they could no longer tolerate the Prophet (pbuh) and plotted to kill him. At this point, Allah permitted migration.
*   **Concept Definition:** Define *Hijrah* (migration). Emphasize that it was not a flight of fear, but a strategic move to build a safe space for Islam.
*   **Language Tip:** Explain *Bay'at al-'Aqabah* (Pledge of 'Aqabah). The people of Yathrib promised to protect the Prophet (pbuh) as they would protect their own families.

---

# Slide 4: Trust (Tawakkul) & Means (Asbab)
## The Ash'ari Creed Perspective on Cause and Effect
*   **Understanding Asbab (أَسْبَاب):**
    *   *Asbab* (singular: *Sabab*) are the physical, worldly means or causes (e.g., preparing food, lock on a door).
*   **Understanding Tawakkul (تَوَكُّل):**
    *   Absolute reliance and trust in Allah as the Sole Creator of all outcomes.
*   **The Ash'ari Middle Path:**
    *   **Rule:** We are commanded to use the *Asbab* (means) with our physical bodies, but we must never believe that the *Asbab* themselves create the result. Only Allah (*Al-Khaliq*) creates the result.
    *   Relying on means without trusting Allah is a form of hidden association (*Shirk Khafi*).
    *   Ignoring means claiming to "trust Allah" is disobedience to His natural laws (*Sufaha'* / foolishness).

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Ash'ari Creed Integration:** This is a crucial theological point. Ash'aris teach that physical causes do not possess independent power to produce effects. Fire does not burn by its own power; Allah creates the burning when the fire touches the wood. 
*   **Application to Seerah:** Show that the Prophet (pbuh) did not just say "Allah will save me" and walk out of Makkah in broad daylight with no plan. He hid, used a guide, took supplies, and took precautions. He used the *Asbab* perfectly, yet his heart relied solely on Allah.
*   **Reflection:** Ask: *"If you study hard for an exam (using the means), who actually grants you the success? Does the studying itself create the grade, or is it Allah?"*

---

# Slide 5: Meticulous Planning: Putting Asbab into Practice
## The Prophet's Strategy
*   **Hiring a Guide:**
    *   The Prophet (pbuh) and Abu Bakr hired Abdullah ibn Urayqit, a non-Muslim skilled guide, showing that expertise is valued regardless of creed.
*   **The Alternative Route:**
    *   Traveling south toward Yemen instead of north toward Madinah to confuse the Quraysh search parties.
*   **The Cave of Thawr:**
    *   Hiding in the cave for three days until the initial search cooled down.
*   **Covering Tracks:**
    *   Amir ibn Fuhayrah grazed Abu Bakr’s sheep behind them to erase their footprints in the sand.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Analysis:** Walk the students through the details of the plan. Highlight how organized it was. This demonstrates that using *Asbab* is part of the Sunnah.
*   **Discussion Point:** Why did the Prophet (pbuh) hire a non-Muslim guide? Explain that in matters of worldly expertise (like navigation or medicine), Muslims are encouraged to seek the best help available, showing that cooperation across beliefs is part of the Sunnah.

---

# Slide 6: Sacrifice on the Night of Hijrah
## Ali ibn Abi Talib’s Bravery
*   **The Plot:**
    *   Quraysh selected a youth from every tribe to strike the Prophet (pbuh) simultaneously, dividing the blood-guilt.
*   **The Sacrifice:**
    *   Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah honor him) volunteered to sleep in the Prophet's bed, wearing his green cloak, acting as a decoy.
*   **Fulfilling Trusts (*Amanat*):**
    *   Even though the Quraysh were trying to kill him, they had left their valuables with the Prophet (pbuh) because of his honesty (*Al-Amin*).
    *   Ali was instructed to stay behind to return every single trust (*Amanah*) to its Makkan owner.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Ethical Focus:** Emphasize the Prophet’s (pbuh) character. Even when his enemies wanted to assassinate him, he refused to steal their property. He ensured all their belongings were safely returned.
*   **Sacrifice lesson:** Talk about the courage of Ali. He knew he might be killed, yet his love for the Prophet (pbuh) and trust in Allah overcame his fear.
*   **Fiqh Connection:** This highlights the absolute obligation (*Fard*) of returning trusts (*Amanah*) to their owners, even if the owners are non-Muslim combatants or enemies.

---

# Slide 7: Friendship and Sacrifice in the Cave
## Abu Bakr al-Siddiq’s Loyalty
*   **Entering the Cave First:**
    *   Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) entered the Cave of Thawr first to clean it and block all holes to protect the Prophet (pbuh) from snakes and scorpions.
*   **The Quraysh at the Entrance:**
    *   The trackers reached the very mouth of the cave.
    *   Abu Bakr whispered: *"If one of them looks down at his feet, he will see us."*
*   **Prophetic Certainty (*Yaqeen*):**
    *   The Prophet (pbuh) replied: *"O Abu Bakr, what do you think of two, of whom Allah is the third?"* (Quran 9:40).
*   **The Miracle of the Spider and the Dove:**
    *   Allah used a spider web and a nesting dove (weak causes) to turn away the heavily armed trackers.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Theological lesson:** Discuss how Allah uses the weakest of *Asbab* (a spider's web) to defeat the strongest army. This proves that outcomes are created by Allah, not by the strength of the physical cause.
*   **Virtue of Abu Bakr:** Explain why Abu Bakr is called *Al-Siddiq* (The Truthful/Believing). His companionship (*Suhbah*) in the cave is explicitly mentioned in the Quran.
*   **Reflection:** How does true friendship look in times of danger?

---

# Slide 8: Arrival in Yathrib
## The Birth of Al-Madinah al-Munawwarah
*   **The Arrival:**
    *   The Prophet (pbuh) arrived in Quba' on 12th Rabi' al-Awwal, founding the first mosque there, before entering Yathrib.
*   **A New Name:**
    *   Yathrib was renamed **Al-Madinah al-Munawwarah** (الْمَدِينَة الْمُنَوَّرَة) — "The Illuminated City" or simply **Al-Madinah** (The City).
*   **The Prophet's Camel (*Al-Qaswa'*):**
    *   To avoid playing favorites among the tribes who wanted him to stay with them, the Prophet (pbuh) let his camel walk freely: *"Let her go, for she is commanded."*
    *   She knelt at the plot belonging to two young orphans, which became the site of the Prophet's Mosque.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Historical detail:** Explain that "Yathrib" had a connotation of sickness or blame in Arabic, so the Prophet (pbuh) renamed it. Renaming places with positive names is a Sunnah.
*   **Wisdom in camel's choice:** Highlight the Prophet's (pbuh) political wisdom. By letting the camel choose, he avoided tribal jealousy among the Ansar.
*   **Fiqh Note:** The Prophet (pbuh) insisted on paying the orphans for the land, refusing to take it as a charity. This teaches the importance of protecting the wealth of orphans (*Aytam*) in Islamic law.

---

# Slide 9: The First Action: Building the Mosque
## The Center of the Community
*   **Al-Masjid al-Nabawi (الْمَسْجِد النَّبَوِيّ):**
    *   Built from clay bricks and palm trunks. The Prophet (pbuh) worked alongside the companions, carrying bricks.
*   **Multi-functional Center:**
    *   Not just a place for ritual prayer (*Salah*).
    *   A school/university for the students of the *Suffah*.
    *   A court of law and assembly hall for community decisions.
    *   A hospital for the sick and wounded.
*   **Equality in Action:**
    *   All Muslims, rich and poor, black and white, Arab and non-Arab, stood shoulder-to-shoulder in the same row.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Sociological impact:** Emphasize that the Mosque was the heart of the community. In the modern world, mosques are often seen only as places to pray. In the Prophetic era, they were the center of civic, educational, and social life.
*   **The Suffah:** Explain who the *Ahl al-Suffah* were (poor companions who lived in the mosque courtyard, dedicating themselves to learning). They became the prime transmitters of Hadith (like Abu Hurayrah).

---

# Slide 10: Establishing Brotherhood (Al-Muwakhah)
## Healing the Fractured Society
*   **The Two Groups:**
    *   **Al-Muhajirun (الْمُهَاجِرُونَ):** The Emigrants who left Makkah with nothing.
    *   **Al-Ansar (الأَنْصَار):** The Helpers of Madinah who welcomed them.
*   **The Muwakhah (الْمُؤَاخَاة):**
    *   The Prophet (pbuh) paired each Muhajir with an Ansari as brothers.
*   **Extreme Generosity:**
    *   The Ansar offered to split their houses, lands, and wealth in half with their new brothers.
*   **Dignity of the Muhajirun:**
    *   The Muhajirun did not rely on charity permanently. Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf said: *"Show me the way to the market,"* and began trading.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Social Engineering:** Explain how the Prophet (pbuh) solved the refugee crisis. Instead of building refugee camps, he integrated the Muhajirun directly into families.
*   **Moral Lesson:** Emphasize the balance between the generosity of the Ansar and the dignity/work ethic of the Muhajirun.
*   **Discussion:** How can we show the spirit of *Ansar* to new students or refugees in our modern communities?

---

# Slide 11: The Constitution of Madinah
## Wathiqat al-Madinah: A Document of Peace
*   **The Document:**
    *   An agreement drafted by the Prophet (pbuh) establishing the rules of the city.
*   **A Unified Nation (*Ummah Wahidah*):**
    *   The treaty declared all signatories (Muslims of Quraysh and Yathrib, and the Jewish tribes) to be "one community (*Ummah*) to the exclusion of all other people."
*   **Freedom of Belief:**
    *   *"The Jews have their religion and the Muslims have theirs."*
*   **Mutual Defense:**
    *   All citizens promised to defend Madinah collectively if it was attacked.
*   **Rule of Law:**
    *   Arbitration of disputes was referred back to the Prophet (pbuh).

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Historical Significance:** Point out that this is considered by historians to be the first written constitution in human history.
*   **Terminology:** *Wathiqat al-Madinah* (وَثِيقَة الْمَدِينَة) or *Kitab al-Madinah*. 
*   **Clarification:** Make sure students understand that the word *Ummah* here was used in a civic sense—a coalition of citizens bound by mutual defense, even though they held different religious beliefs. This teaches that Muslims can form civic coalitions with non-Muslims for the common good.

---

# Slide 12: Living with Different Communities
## Civic Duty and Pluralism
*   **Jewish Tribes of Madinah:**
    *   Banu Qaynuqa', Banu al-Nadir, and Banu Qurayzah.
*   **Rights of Non-Muslim Citizens:**
    *   Protection of life, property, and freedom of worship.
    *   No forced conversion to Islam.
*   **Responsibilities:**
    *   Contributing financially to the defense of the city during warfare.
    *   Refraining from aiding the external enemies of Madinah (like the Quraysh).
*   **Justice for All:**
    *   The Prophet (pbuh) said: *"Beware, whoever oppresses a covenant-partner (Mu'ahid) or cuts off his right... I will be his opponent on the Day of Resurrection"* (Abu Dawud).

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Civic Education:** Teach students that Islam respects diversity. The Prophet (pbuh) did not expel the Jewish tribes or force them to convert upon his arrival. He made them equal partners in the city's defense.
*   **Terminology:** *Mu'ahid* (مُعَاهِد) — a non-Muslim who belongs to a community that has a treaty or covenant with the Muslims.
*   **Concept Check:** What were the obligations of the non-Muslims? (Defense contribution, non-treason). What were their rights? (Safety, freedom of religion).

---

# Slide 13: Fiqh of Treaties and Covenants
## Maliki Jurisprudence on International Agreements
*   **Sanctity of Treaties (*'Ahd*):**
    *   In Maliki fiqh, breaking a covenant or treaty (*'Ahd* - عَهْد) is a major sin. Treaties must be honored unless the other party explicitly betrays them.
*   **The Principle of Safety (*Aman* - أَمَان):**
    *   If a single Muslim (man or woman) grants protection/safety to a non-Muslim traveler, the entire Muslim community and state must honor that safety.
    *   Imam Malik ruled that even the word or gesture of safety from a common citizen is legally binding.
*   **Treachery (*Ghadr* - غَدْر):**
    *   Strictly forbidden. Muslims cannot attack an enemy while a treaty is active, nor use deception to bypass a peace treaty.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Maliki Specificity:** Highlight Imam Malik’s ruling in the *Muwatta* that if a Muslim makes a sign or gesture that looks like safety to a non-Muslim, that non-Muslim is protected. This shows how high the Maliki school values the word and honor of a believer, and how much it protects human life.
*   **Key Concept:** *Aman* (protection/safety) and *'Ahd* (covenant). Explain that treaties are not just political tools but sacred legal obligations before Allah.

---

# Slide 14: The Shift to Defense
## Understanding the Permission for Battle
*   **The Makkan Period Rule:**
    *   Muslims were commanded to hold back their hands and only establish prayer (*Kuffu aydiyakum*).
*   **The Madinan Period Permission:**
    *   After 13 years of oppression, theft of property, and exile, Allah revealed:
    *   *"Permission [to fight] has been given to those who are being fought, because they were wronged..."* (Quran 22:39).
*   **The Purpose of Fighting (*Qital*):**
    *   Strictly defensive: To defend against aggression.
    *   Preservative: To protect places of worship—monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques (Quran 22:40).
    *   Not for forced conversion: *"There is no compulsion in religion"* (Quran 2:256).

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Anti-Radicalization & Fiqh Literacy:** It is vital to teach that fighting (*Qital*) was permitted only to repel aggression and protect the innocent. Explain Quran 22:40: the Quran explicitly says fighting was allowed so that churches, synagogues, and mosques would not be destroyed. This means Islamic defense protects the religious freedom of others.
*   **Term Check:** Differentiate between *Jihad* (which means striving in all good ways, like studying or fighting our desires) and *Qital* (specifically physical combat in self-defense).

---

# Slide 15: Battle of Badr: The Test of Yaqeen
## Faith vs. Physical Might
*   **The Context (2 AH):**
    *   Quraysh sent a massive army of 1,000 soldiers to crush Madinah. The Muslims were only 313, poorly equipped.
*   **Consultation (*Shura* - شُورَى):**
    *   The Prophet (pbuh) consulted the Ansar, as they had promised to protect him in Madinah, not fight outside.
    *   Sa'd ibn Mu'adh (leader of Ansar) said: *"If you lead us to the sea and plunge into it, we will plunge with you!"*
*   **The Night Before Badr:**
    *   While the army slept peacefully, the Prophet (pbuh) spent the entire night weeping and praying to Allah for victory.
*   **The Result:**
    *   Despite being outnumbered 3 to 1, the Muslims won a decisive victory.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Moral Lessons:**
    *   *Shura* (consultation): The Prophet (pbuh) did not act like a dictator. He consulted his community, especially the Ansar, respecting their treaty boundaries.
    *   *Yaqeen* (certainty): Trusting Allah when the odds seem impossible.
*   **Discussion:** Why did Allah make the Muslims win at Badr? Was it because of their swords, or because of their spiritual connection and surrender to Him?

---

# Slide 16: The Source of Victory
## Ash'ari Creed: Who Creates the Outcome?
*   **The Quranic Verse:**
    *   *"And you threw not when you threw, but it was Allah who threw..."* (Quran 8:17).
*   **Creed Focus: Divine Will and Creation:**
    *   In Ash'ari theology, Allah is the Sole Creator of all actions. 
    *   The Prophet (pbuh) threw a handful of dust at the enemy (the *Sabab*/cause), but it was Allah who made that dust reach the eyes of every soldier in the enemy army (the *Musabbib*/effect creator).
*   **The Angels at Badr:**
    *   Allah sent 1,000 angels to assist, not because Allah needs angels, but to bring tranquility (*Sakinah*) to the hearts of the believers.
*   **Lesson:** Victory does not come from numbers or weapons; it comes only from Allah (*Al-Nasir*).

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Ash'ari Creed Integration:** Explain Quran 8:17. The physical throwing was attributed to the Prophet (pbuh) as an acquisition (*Kasb*), but the ultimate creation of the action's effect was attributed to Allah.
*   **Relevance:** When we win or succeed, we must not become arrogant. We must thank Allah, because He is the source of all success.
*   **Concept Definition:** *Al-Nasir* (النَّاصِر) — The Giver of Victory.

---

# Slide 17: Battle of Uhud: Obedience & Sabr
## The Test of Spiritual Discipline
*   **The Context (3 AH):**
    *   Quraysh returned with 3,000 soldiers to avenge Badr.
*   **The Archers' Command:**
    *   The Prophet (pbuh) stationed 50 archers on Mount Aynayn, commanding them: *"Do not leave your post, even if you see birds pecking our corpses, until I send for you."*
*   **The Mistake:**
    *   When the battle seemed won, the archers saw the spoils of war (*Ghanimah*) and rushed down, leaving their post unprotected.
*   **The Setback:**
    *   Khalid ibn al-Walid (then commanding the Quraysh cavalry) attacked from behind, turning victory into defeat. The Prophet (pbuh) was wounded.
*   **The Lesson:**
    *   Disobedience to the Prophetic command and loving worldly gain (*Dunya*) leads to spiritual and physical setbacks.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Analysis:** Emphasize that Uhud was not a failure of strategy, but a failure of spiritual discipline.
*   **Creed Angle:** Why did Allah allow them to suffer? To teach them that victory is tied to obedience and patience (*Sabr*). It also proved the human nature of the Prophet (pbuh); he was wounded, showing he is a human messenger, not a divine being (refuting extremist beliefs).
*   **Reflection:** Ask: *"Can you think of a time when you disobeyed a rule because you wanted something quick, and it ended up ruining things for you?"*

---

# Slide 18: Ethics of Warfare in the Maliki School
## Islamic Rules of Engagement
*   **Imam Malik's Rulings on Combat:**
    *   Strictly prohibited: Killing women, children, the elderly, monks/priests in their monasteries, and non-combatants.
    *   Strictly prohibited: Cutting down fruitful trees, destroying crops, killing livestock (except for food), and burning property.
    *   Prohibited: Poisoning wells or using weapons of mass destruction that kill indiscriminately.
*   **Comparison:**
    *   While modern international law (Geneva Conventions) was written in the 20th century, these rules were laid down by the Prophet (pbuh) and formalized by Imam Malik 1,300 years ago.
*   **The Goal of Battle:**
    *   Restoring peace and justice, not vengeance or looting.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Fiqh Literacy Focus:** Cite Imam Malik's rulings from the *Muwatta*. When Abu Bakr sent the army to Syria, he gave a famous 10-point command summarizing these rules. Imam Malik recorded this and codified it into law.
*   **Ethics Discussion:** Contrast this with the "scorched earth" policies of ancient empires (and some modern nations). Islam completely bans destroying nature during war.
*   **Key Arabic Term:** *Qital* (قِتَال) vs. *Harb* (حَرْب - war).

---

# Slide 19: The Farewell Sermon (Khutbat al-Wada')
## The Final Message of Equality and Justice
*   **The Context (10 AH):**
    *   During the final pilgrimage, the Prophet (pbuh) addressed over 100,000 companions at Mount Arafat.
*   **Sacredness of Human Life & Property:**
    *   *"Your blood and your property are sacred to you, like the sacredness of this day..."*
*   **Abolition of Riba (Usury/Interest):**
    *   Economic justice: Stopping exploitative money-lending systems that keep the poor in debt.
*   **Eradication of Racism:**
    *   *"An Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab; a white person has no superiority over a black person, nor a black over a white, except by piety (Taqwa)."*
*   **Rights of Women:**
    *   *"Fear Allah concerning women, for you have taken them as a trust (Amanah) from Allah."*

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Significance:** This sermon is the final summary of the Prophet's (pbuh) mission. It serves as a universal declaration of human rights.
*   **Interactive Reading:** Read the quotes aloud with deep respect. 
*   **Discussion:** Why is usury (*Riba*) mentioned alongside the sacredness of blood? Explain that economic oppression kills communities slowly, just like physical violence.

---

# Slide 20: Protecting the Five Necessities
## Al-Daruriyyat al-Khams: The Goals of Shariah
*   The Farewell Sermon established laws to protect the **Five Necessities (*Al-Daruriyyat al-Khams* - الضَّرُورِيَّات الْخَمْس)**:
    1.  **Preservation of Religion (*Hifz al-Din*):** Freedom of worship.
    2.  **Preservation of Life (*Hifz al-Nafs*):** Sanctity of blood.
    3.  **Preservation of Intellect (*Hifz al-'Aql*):** Protection against toxins.
    4.  **Preservation of Lineage/Honor (*Hifz al-Nasl*):** Sanctity of family.
    5.  **Preservation of Wealth (*Hifz al-Mal*):** Prohibiting theft and *Riba*.
*   Every law in Maliki fiqh is designed to protect one or more of these five pillars.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Fiqh Literacy / Maqasid:** Introduce the concept of *Maqasid al-Shariah* (the objectives of Islamic Law). Teach the students that Islamic laws are not random rules to restrict us; they are designed to protect these 5 essential elements of human life.
*   **Language Tip:** Write *Al-Daruriyyat al-Khams* on the board and go through each one with a concrete example.

---

# Slide 21: From the Companions to Imam Malik
## How Knowledge Travelled to Madinah
*   **The Transmission of Sunnah:**
    *   The Prophet (pbuh) lived and died in Madinah.
    *   His companions (like Umar, Ibn Umar, Aisha, Zayd ibn Thabit) stayed in Madinah and taught the next generation.
*   **The Seven Fiqh Scholars of Madinah:**
    *   The top students of the Sahabah who consolidated the law in the generation of the Tabi'un (e.g., Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Urwah ibn al-Zubayr).
*   **The Teacher of Imam Malik:**
    *   Nafi' (the freed slave of Ibn Umar) and Rabi'at al-Ra'y.
*   **Imam Malik ibn Anas (93–179 AH):**
    *   The "Imam of the Abode of Emigration" (*Imam Dar al-Hijrah*). He compiled the rulings of Madinah in his book *Al-Muwatta*.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **The Chain of Knowledge:** Draw or trace the path of transmission.
    *   Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) -> Ibn Umar / Aisha -> Nafi' -> Imam Malik.
    *   This is known as the **Golden Chain** (*Silsilat al-Dhahab*).
*   **Pedagogical point:** Explain why the Maliki school relies so heavily on this chain. It is a direct, living chain of action, not just books.

---

# Slide 22: 'Amal Ahl al-Madinah (Practice of Madinah)
## The Living Sunnah
*   **What is 'Amal Ahl al-Madinah (عَمَل أَهْل الْمَدِينَة)?**
    *   The continuous, mass-transmitted practices of the people of Madinah.
*   **Imam Malik's Logic:**
    *   If thousands of people in Madinah (the children of the Sahabah) perform an action (like the Adhan, or not crossing hands in prayer), it is more reliable than a report from a single person (*Khabar al-Wahid*).
    *   Living practice acts like a "mass-transmitted Hadith" (*Mutawatir*).
*   **The Fiqh Literacy Lesson:**
    *   Understanding *'Amal* helps us see why Malikis might differ in some physical actions of prayer or business, based on this strong city-wide inheritance.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Fiqh Literacy Focus:** Explain the concept of *'Amal Ahl al-Madinah*. Use the example of a school policy: *"If the principal tells the whole school to do something, and everyone does it every day, it is more reliable than one student claiming the principal told him something different in private."*
*   **Sadl Example:** The posture of letting arms hang at the sides (*Sadl*) in obligatory prayer is based on *'Amal Ahl al-Madinah*—the continuous practice of the city's scholars who learned from the Sahabah.

---

# Slide 23: Course Summary & Sources
## Building on the Legacy of Madinah
*   **Key Lessons:**
    *   Trust Allah while utilizing the means (*Asbab*).
    *   Live peacefully in diverse societies through justice and covenants.
    *   Understand conflict as a test of patience, never glorify war.
    *   Protect human rights as outlined in the Farewell Sermon.
    *   Honor the chain of knowledge from the Prophet (pbuh) to Imam Malik.
*   **Core Sources for Study:**
    *   *Al-Muwatta* — Imam Malik
    *   *Al-Shifa* — Qadi 'Ayyad
    *   *Al-Seerah al-Nabawiyyah* — Ibn Hisham
    *   *Fiqh al-Seerah* — Muhammad al-Ghazali
    *   *Introduction to Islamic Creed* — Ash'ari scholars

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Final Wrap-up:** Congratulate the students. Encourage them to see themselves as part of this continuous chain of knowledge that began in Madinah.
*   **Assessment Prep:** Tell the students to prepare for the assessment questions based on these slides and their handouts.

# Slide 1: Welcome & Course Overview
## Building the Sacred Community
*   **Subject:** Islamic History (*Seerah*) and Jurisprudence (*Fiqh*)
*   **Fiqh School:** Maliki (*Madhhab*)
*   **Creed School:** Ash'ari (*Aqidah*)
*   **Core Focus:** Understanding the migration (*Hijrah*) to Madinah, the founding of the Islamic state, the rules of peaceful coexistence, the reality of defensive warfare, and the transmission of knowledge down to Imam Malik.
*   **Key Themes:**
    *   Trust in Allah (*Tawakkul*) and using physical means (*Asbab*)
    *   The Constitution of Madinah (*Wathiqat al-Madinah*)
    *   Patience in trials: Badr and Uhud
    *   The Farewell Sermon and the five necessities of Shariah (*Al-Daruriyyat al-Khams*)
    *   The Practice of the People of Madinah (*'Amal Ahl al-Madinah*)

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Welcome & Objective:** Welcome the students to this unit. Explain that this course moves from the Makkan period (which focused on personal belief in Tawheed) to the Madinan period, where those beliefs were put into action to build a community.
*   **Pedagogical Note:** Highlight that we study the Seerah not just as historical events, but as the foundation of our *Fiqh* (law) and *Aqidah* (creed). We will pay special attention to the rulings of the Maliki school and theological explanations of the Ash'ari school to show how classical scholars derived truth from the Prophet's life.
*   **Discussion Starter:** Ask the class: *"If you were starting a brand new town with people of different religions, what is the very first rule or agreement you would make?"*

# Slide 2: Fiqh & Aqidah Framework: The Madinan Context
## Connecting History to Belief and Practice
*   **Aqidah (Creed) Context:**
    *   The transition from forming the creed (*Tawheed*) in Makkah to manifesting it in community life.
    *   Understanding Divine Decree (*Qadar*) in times of victory and defeat.
*   **Fiqh (Law) Context:**
    *   Madinah is the birthplace of the Sunnah's practical implementation.
    *   Imam Malik’s jurisprudence is built on the living practice of this very city (*'Amal Ahl al-Madinah*).
*   **Seerah as Law:**
    *   The actions, treaties, and battles of the Prophet (pbuh) in Madinah became the legal bases for international relations, contracts, and governance.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Explanation:** Explain that in Makkah, Muslims had no state or political power; they focused on purifying their hearts and establishing *Aqidah*. In Madinah, Allah established them in the land. Thus, laws (*Fiqh*) regarding family, business, treaties, and community cooperation were revealed.
*   **Ash'ari/Maliki Link:** Emphasize that for Malikis, the customs and continuous practice of Madinah's early generations are highly authoritative. This is because they inherited their daily practices directly from the Prophet (pbuh) without interruption.

---
